result: Pregnant mice show a rapid, profound reduction in voluntary running wheel activity (RWA) starting on the first day of pregnancy, persisting throughout pregnancy and lactation, with a brief increase on the day of birth. This reduction is robust and independent of wheel type (upright vs. saucer).
evaluation: Claims C1, C13-C15, C17-C20 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1 showing RWA measurements across reproductive states with appropriate statistical analyses (p<0.0001). The data demonstrate consistent effects across different wheel types and include sufficient sample sizes (n=35 upright, n=27 saucer). The brief increase on day of birth (C19-C20) is well-documented with 88% of mice showing this effect.

result: Early pregnancy is associated with reduced physical activity independent of activity type, as demonstrated by significant reductions in both energy expenditure and home cage ambulation in mice without running wheels, and major reductions in RWA when wheels are present.
evaluation: Claims C22-C26 are supported by experimental data from metabolic cages (Figure 1E-G) showing significant reductions in both energy expenditure (p=0.03) and ambulation (p=0.03) in early pregnancy. The inference that RWA represents the predominant form of activity when wheels are present (C25-C26) is reasonable given the magnitude of effects observed.

result: Acute prolactin treatment (5 mg/kg i.p.) significantly suppresses RWA in female mice, particularly in the first 3 hours of the dark phase, but has no effect in male mice. Female mice run significantly more than males under control conditions.
evaluation: Claims C2, C28-C30 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2 with appropriate statistical analyses showing significant reduction in female RWA (p=0.007) but not males (p=0.8732), and sex differences in baseline RWA (p<0.0001). The counterbalanced design with n=12 per sex provides adequate power.

result: Prolactin reduces voluntary RWA in female mice but has minimal effects on general locomotion in novel environments or home cage ambulation. Prolactin increases fine (non-ambulatory) movements while having subtle or no effects on directed ambulation.
evaluation: Claims C31-C38 are supported by experimental data from multiple behavioral assays (Figures 3A-G). The lack of effect on distance traveled in EPM and OFT (C31-C32) is well-documented. The subtle effect on home cage ambulation (C33, p=0.016) contrasts with the robust increase in fine movements (C35, p<0.0001), supporting the inference that prolactin specifically affects voluntary exercise rather than general locomotion.

result: Conditional deletion of Prlr from most forebrain neurons (Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre) prevents the early pregnancy-induced suppression of RWA and results in significantly higher RWA throughout pregnancy compared to controls, independent of body weight differences.
evaluation: Claims C3, C62-C68 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing that Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice fail to show RWA suppression in early pregnancy (p=0.3899 for time effect) while controls show ~50% reduction (p=0.002). The effect persists in late pregnancy (p<0.0001) and is independent of body weight as demonstrated by ANCOVA (p=0.0006). Sample sizes are adequate (n=12-15).

result: Conditional deletion of Prlr from GABA neurons (Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre) prevents early pregnancy-induced RWA suppression, but unlike forebrain deletion, the effect diminishes in late pregnancy, suggesting GABAergic neurons mediate early but not late pregnancy effects.
evaluation: Claims C4, C80-C81, C85-C88 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice fail to suppress RWA in early pregnancy (p=0.7888 for time effect) but show similar RWA to controls by days 16-18 (p=0.1728). This temporal pattern differs from the forebrain deletion model, supporting the inference that different neuronal populations mediate early vs. late pregnancy effects.

result: Region-specific deletion of Prlr from the medial preoptic area (MPOA) using AAV-cre completely abolishes early pregnancy-induced RWA suppression and maintains elevated RWA throughout pregnancy. This manipulation also causes maternal behavior failure and pup abandonment.
evaluation: Claims C5, C107-C112 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing complete loss of prolactin signaling in MPOA (pSTAT5 staining), failure of RWA suppression in early pregnancy (p=0.9687 for time effect in AAV-cre group vs. p=0.01 in controls), and 100% pup abandonment (p<0.0001). The data strongly support the MPOA as a critical site for prolactin-mediated RWA suppression.

result: Deletion of Prlr from arcuate nucleus kisspeptin neurons (Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre) produces only a subtle attenuation of early pregnancy RWA suppression, suggesting kisspeptin neurons make a minor contribution to this response.
evaluation: Claims C97-C99, C139-C140 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing both genotypes suppress RWA in early pregnancy, but the effect is subtly reduced in Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice (p=0.0049 for genotype effect in early pregnancy). The small effect size and lack of difference in later pregnancy (C99) support the inference that kisspeptin neurons play only a minor role.

result: Prolactin action contributes to RWA suppression in early lactation (days 1-3) but is not necessary for sustained suppression throughout lactation, as evidenced by higher RWA in Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice only in early lactation.
evaluation: Claims C115-C118 are supported by experimental data in Figure 7 showing significantly higher RWA in Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice on days 1-3 of lactation (p<0.0001 for genotype effect) but no difference for most of lactation (p>0.05 for days 2-20). The observation of breakthrough high RWA days in 3/5 knockout mice (C118) provides additional evidence for prolactin's role.

result: Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice exhibit abnormal estrous cycles with serial pseudopregnancy-like phases due to hyperprolactinemia, show absence of cyclical RWA patterns, but have similar cumulative 5-day RWA to controls despite slightly increased body weight.
evaluation: Claims C54-C60 are supported by experimental data showing abnormal estrous cycles (p<0.0001), absence of cyclical RWA patterns (Figure 4C), no difference in cumulative 5-day RWA (p=0.0831), and slightly increased body weight (p=0.0156). These findings are important confounds but don't invalidate the pregnancy results as the cumulative activity levels are similar.

result: Validation studies demonstrate that Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice have significant Prlr reduction from GABAergic neurons in the MPOA, while Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre mice show ~70% deletion of Prlr from GABA neurons, though not complete deletion.
evaluation: Claims C52, C74-C75, C136 are supported by experimental validation data using RNAscope in situ hybridization and pSTAT5 immunohistochemistry (Figures 4—figure supplements 1-2) with appropriate statistical analyses. The incomplete deletion in Slc32a1Cre mice (C75) is an important caveat properly acknowledged by the authors.

result: Multiple distinct prolactin-sensitive pathways regulate RWA across pregnancy stages: GABAergic neurons in the MPOA mediate early pregnancy effects, while non-GABAergic populations contribute to late pregnancy suppression.
evaluation: Claims C6, C143-C148 are supported by the differential temporal patterns observed across knockout models: Slc32a1Cre effects diminish in late pregnancy while Camk2aCre and MPOA-specific deletions persist. This supports the inference of multiple pathways, though the specific non-GABAergic cell types remain unidentified (acknowledged limitation).

result: The study demonstrates that mating-induced prolactin release, acting through brain Prlr, induces marked RWA reduction in early pregnancy that continues throughout pregnancy and early lactation, representing an adaptive metabolic strategy.
evaluation: Claims C122-C124, C173 summarize the main findings supported by the collective experimental data. The interpretation as an adaptive metabolic strategy (C123-C124) is reasonable given the timing before metabolic load increases and is supported by citations to relevant literature on pregnancy metabolism.

result: The findings may have translational relevance to human pregnancy, as prolactin/placental lactogen are highly regulated during human pregnancy, and the mechanism may contribute to the disconnect between knowledge and action regarding exercise during pregnancy.
evaluation: Claims C125-C132, C177, C181-C183 involve speculation about human relevance. While the background on human pregnancy and exercise is well-cited (C126-C131), the direct applicability of the mouse findings to humans is uncertain. The authors appropriately acknowledge this requires further investigation (C177). The speculation is reasonable but not experimentally validated in the current study.

result: Knockout mice (Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre and Prlrlox/lox/Slc32a1Cre) show normal pregnancy outcomes including similar litter sizes, food intake, and no differences in anxiety-like behavior compared to controls.
evaluation: Claims C61, C70-C71, C78, C82-C83 are supported by experimental data showing no significant differences in fetus number, uterus mass, litter size, food intake, or EPM performance between genotypes. This is important for ruling out general health or stress effects as confounds for the RWA phenotype.

result: Other factors beyond prolactin, potentially including progesterone or suckling-induced neural inputs, may contribute to sustained RWA suppression during lactation, though this remains speculative.
evaluation: Claims C164-C172 are largely speculative about mechanisms not directly tested in the study. While the speculation is informed by relevant literature (C165-C168, C171), these hypotheses require experimental validation. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities rather than conclusions.

result: Despite losing only ~50% of Prlr in the MPOA, Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice show attenuated RWA suppression but can still care for offspring, suggesting the neurons controlling RWA are a subset of or distinct from those required for maternal behavior.
evaluation: Claims C153-C155 are supported by the contrasting phenotypes: MPOA-specific deletion causes complete maternal behavior failure while forebrain deletion (with partial MPOA deletion) allows pup care despite RWA effects. This supports the inference of distinct or partially overlapping neuronal populations, though the exact relationship requires further investigation.
